spec.full_target:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
spec.conclusion: dim_H(E × [0,1]) = dim_H E + 1, where E × [0,1] is identified with Eucl(n+1) by adjoining the last coordinate and carries the Euclidean metric. Equivalently, dim_H F = D+1.

hypotheses.statement: E is compact in the Euclidean topology on Eucl(n).

definitions.type: family of metric topological spaces indexed by natural numbers
definitions.definition: For a natural number m, Eucl(m)=R^m is the space of real coordinate vectors indexed by {0,...,m-1}; distance between x and y is (sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(x_k-y_k)^2)^(1/2). The topology is generated by open balls for this distance. In particular Eucl(0) has exactly one vector, the empty tuple. Identify Eucl(m) × R with Eucl(m+1) by (x,t)↦(x_0,...,x_{m-1},t); its distance is sqrt(dist(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2), not the maximum product distance. Compact means that every cover by open sets has a finite subcover.

definitions.type: extended nonnegative real diameter of a subset of a metric space
definitions.definition: diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y): x,y∈A}, with diameter zero for A empty. For sets of finite diameter it is the usual nonnegative real diameter. All covers at a finite scale have finite diameters. For s>0 the cost of an empty set or a diameter-zero set is 0^s=0.

definitions.type: scale Hausdorff contents and Hausdorff measures on Euclidean subsets, valued in [0,∞]
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This

binders.type: countable family of subsets of that space

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of a Euclidean subset, valued in [0,∞]
definitions.definition: dim_H A is inf{s∈R: s>0 and H^s(A)=0}, as an infimum in [0,∞], with infimum of the empty set infinity. In particular dim_H(empty)=0. Dimension inequalities against real numbers use their nonnegative extended-real values. Once finiteness has been proved the same symbols are also used for their real values.
F=E×I={(x,t):x∈E, t∈I}, using the coordinate-adjoining Euclidean identification of D001.
D=dim_H E. Its finiteness and bound by n are conclusions to be proved, not conditions of this definition.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on R with its Borel measurable structure
definitions.definition: λ denotes the standard Lebesgue measure on the Borel sigma algebra of R (used also as its outer measure on arbitrary sets). For a nonnegative Borel function, ∫ g dλ denotes its extended nonnegative Lebesgue integral. Indicator notation 1_T(t) is 1 for t∈T and 0 otherwise. A sum of nonnegative terms denotes the supremum of its finite partial sums and can equal infinity.

For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension. We use
its critical-exponent characterization: \(H^s(A)=0\) if
\(s>\dim_H A\), and \(H^s(A)=\infty\) if \(0<s<\dim_H A\).
Conversely, zero measure implies \(\dim_H A\leq s\), and infinite
measure implies \(\dim_H A\geq s\).

locals.declaration: Choose B≥1 with E⊆[-B,B]^n, using F001.
In the n>0 branch let s>n be arbitrary, to be universally closed in this paragraph.
Let 0<h≤1 be arbitrary in the grid estimate.
Set C=(2B+1)^n.

argument.text: From H002 and the open-cover definition of compactness, the open balls of any fixed positive radius centered at all points of E have a finite subcover. For arbitrary s>0 and δ>0, apply this with radius δ/2. Every such ball has diameter at most δ by the triangle inequality, and the resulting finite δ-cover has finite s-cost, proving H^s_δ(E)<∞. Similarly a finite subcover by radius-one balls bounds E: each ball is contained in the box whose coordinate bounds are the absolute coordinates of its center plus one. The finite maximum of these coordinate bounds, increased to at least one, gives a real B≥1 with E⊆[-B,B]^n. If E has no centers the conclusion also holds with B=1, although H001 excludes that case. Thus the existence in F001 is established without presupposing boundedness.

produces.statement: There exists a real B≥1 such that E⊆[-B,B]^n; also for every s>0 and δ>0, H^s_δ(E)<∞.

argument.text: Choose B as in F001. In the case L1: n>0, fix s>n and 0<h≤1. Divide each coordinate interval [-B,B] into ceil(2B/h) equal closed pieces, each of length at most h. Their products cover the box and hence E. The number of cubes is at most ((2B+1)/h)^n=C h^(-n), where C=(2B+1)^n, independent of h. The Euclidean diameter of each is at most sqrt(n)h, by the sum-of-squares distance formula. Their total s-cost is at most C n^(s/2)h^(s-n), which tends to zero as h decreases to zero since s-n>0. Given any target scale and any positive cost tolerance, h can be chosen small enough for both requirements. Thus H^s_δ(E)=0 for every δ>0 and H^s(E)=0. E001 then gives D≤s for every s>n; letting s decrease to n gives D≤n. This proves n>0 implies D≤n, and discharges L1. Nonnegativity follows from the nonnegative-infimum definition of dim_H.

In the case L2: n=0, Eucl(0) consists of the empty tuple. H001 therefore gives E=Eucl(0), a singleton. Its diameter is zero, so its one-member cover has zero s-cost at every positive scale for every s>0. Thus H^s(E)=0, and E001 gives D≤s for all s>0. Since D≥0 by definition, D=0. Discharge L2 to obtain the conditional singleton and dimension assertion.

produces.statement: If n=0 then E is the singleton Eucl(0) and D=0.

argument.text: First assume L1: n=0. N001 says E is the singleton Eucl(0) and D=0. Hence the coordinate map ((),t)↦t is an isometry from F onto I. Fix any a>1. Divide I into N equal closed intervals for each positive integer N and take their inverse images in F. Their Euclidean diameters are 1/N, and total a-cost is N(1/N)^a=N^(1-a)→0 as N→∞. Consequently H^a(F)=0, and E001 gives dim_H F≤a for all a>1. It follows dim_H F≤1=D+1. Discharge L1.

For the remaining branch assume L2: n≥1. Fix q and assume L3: q>D. By N001, q>0. E001 gives H^q(E)=0. Fix r,ε and assume L4: 0<r≤1 and ε>0. Since H^q_r(E)=0, its defining infimum supplies an r-cover with q-cost below ε/2. Discard empty members. Any member of zero diameter is a singleton: two distinct points would have positive distance. Replace the singleton at index i≥0 by a ball centered at that point of diameter at most r and with q-cost less than ε·2^(-i-2). Such a positive-radius ball exists because n≥1 and q>0; take radius smaller than r/2 and (ε·2^(-i-2))^(1/q)/2. Its diameter is twice the radius (the first coordinate supplies opposite endpoints as suprema). The sum of the added costs is at most ε/2, since sum_{i≥0}2^(-i-2)=1/2. Original positive-diameter members cost less than ε/2, so the modified countable cover has total cost less than ε and all diameters in (0,r]. This proves the existence in F002.

argument.text: Choose U from F002, and set r_i=diam(U_i), N_i=ceil(1/r_i). Since 0<r_i≤r≤1, N_i is a positive integer, 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. For each i partition I into N_i closed subintervals with endpoints j/N_i, 0≤j≤N_i. The sets U_i×[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], 0≤j<N_i, give a countable cover of F. For any two points of one such set, the first-coordinate distance is at most r_i and the last-coordinate distance at most 1/N_i≤r_i. D001 therefore bounds its Euclidean diameter by sqrt(2)r_i.

produces.statement: The products U_i×[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], indexed by i and integers 0≤j<N_i, cover F countably and each has diameter at most sqrt(2)r_i; also N_i≤2/r_i.

argument.text: By F004 the total (q+1)-cost of this cover is at most sum_i N_i(sqrt(2)r_i)^(q+1) ≤ 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)sum_i r_i^q < 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)ε. Every member has diameter at most sqrt(2)r. Thus for each 0<r≤1 and ε>0 there exists a sqrt(2)r-cover of F with this cost bound. The cover's private identity is no part of the conclusion. Discharge L4 and quantify r and ε to obtain F003.

produces.statement: For every 0<r0≤1 and ε0>0, F has a countable cover of diameters at most sqrt(2)r0 and total (q+1)-cost less than 2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)ε0.

argument.text: Fix any δ>0 and use F003 with r=min(1,δ/sqrt(2)), which is positive. The cover's diameters are at most δ. As ε ranges over arbitrarily small positive numbers, H^(q+1)_δ(F) is bounded by arbitrarily small positive costs, hence is zero. Every positive scale has zero content, so H^(q+1)(F)=0. Since q+1>0, E001 gives dim_H F≤q+1.

F005 holds for every q>D in the n≥1 branch. Discharge L3 and universally quantify q. N001 gives D finite, so letting q decrease to D (or taking q=D+τ for every τ>0) gives dim_H F≤D+1. Discharge L2. The alternatives n=0 and n≥1 exhaust the natural numbers; combine this branch with F001. The upper bound is finite because D≤n.

Fix a real scale δ; its positivity belongs to L1.
Fix any countable covering family V=(V_i), padded with empty sets if finite, under L2 that it covers F and every diameter is at most δ.
Set ρ_i=diam(V_i), with ρ_i=0 for empty V_i.
Set A_i={x: there is t with (x,t)∈V_i}, the first-coordinate projection.
Set B_i={t: there is x with (x,t)∈V_i}, the last-coordinate projection.
Fix a real ε and assume ε>0 under L3.
Define η_i=ε·2^(-i-1)/(1+ρ_i^s).
Define c=H^s_δ(E); N001 gives finiteness under L1.

locals.declaration: Choose the family J=(J_i) supplied by F001, enclosing every B_i.
Set f(t)=c·1_I(t).
Set g_i(t)=ρ_i^s·1_(J_i∩I)(t).

argument.text: Fix real s,δ and assume L1: s>0, δ>0. Put c=H^s_δ(E), finite by N001. Fix an arbitrary sequence V and assume L2: it is a δ-cover of F; finite countable covers can be padded by empty sets. Define ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i and B_i as its first and last coordinate projections. The Euclidean distance formula gives coordinate distances at most the full distance, hence diam(A_i),diam(B_i)≤ρ_i≤δ. Fix ε and assume L3: ε>0. Define η_i=ε·2^(-i-1)/(1+ρ_i^s)>0. For nonempty V_i, B_i is nonempty and bounded (choose one of its points; every other is within δ). Its real infimum and supremum exist and sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i by the diameter bound. The open interval (inf B_i-η_i/2, sup B_i+η_i/2) contains B_i and has length ≤ρ_i+η_i. For empty V_i use the empty set instead. Thus the sequence of open enclosing intervals required in F001 exists. No measurability of V_i,A_i or B_i is asserted or needed.

produces.statement: There exists a sequence J such that if V_i is nonempty then J_i is a bounded open interval containing B_i with length at most ρ_i+η_i, and if V_i is empty then J_i is empty.

argument.text: Choose J from F001. For arbitrary t∈I and x∈E, (x,t)∈F, so some V_i contains (x,t). Then x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Hence the A_i with t∈J_i cover E. They have diameter at most ρ_i≤δ; pad the remaining indices by empty sets. The definition of c as an infimum of cover costs gives c≤sum_i diam(A_i)^s 1_(J_i)(t)≤sum_i ρ_i^s 1_(J_i)(t). This proves F002 pointwise for all t∈I.

On all of R define f(t)=c·1_I(t) and g_i(t)=ρ_i^s·1_(J_i∩I)(t). F002 gives f≤sum_i g_i, including outside I where both sides vanish. Each J_i is open or empty and I is closed, so J_i∩I is Borel; the nonnegative constant indicators g_i are measurable and hence λ-almost everywhere measurable. Apply M002 to this pointwise inequality and M001 to the measurable nonnegative series. M003 evaluates the constant indicators, and M005 gives λ(I)=1. Thus c=cλ(I)=∫f dλ≤∫sum_i g_i dλ=sum_i∫g_i dλ=sum_i ρ_i^s λ(J_i∩I). By measure monotonicity and M006, λ(J_i∩I)≤λ(J_i)≤ρ_i+η_i (empty intervals have measure zero). It follows that c≤sum_i ρ_i^s(ρ_i+η_i)≤sum_i ρ_i^(s+1)+sum_i η_iρ_i^s≤sum_i ρ_i^(s+1)+ε, since η_iρ_i^s≤ε·2^(-i-1) and sum_{i≥0}2^(-i-1)=1. These inequalities of nonnegative series follow first for finite partial sums and then by their suprema. They include ρ_i=0 because s>0. No interchange of signed or nonmeasurable functions has occurred.

The bound F003 holds for every ε>0, with c and the original V,ρ fixed independently of ε. Discharge L3 and quantify ε. If sum_i ρ_i^(s+1)=∞ then c≤this sum immediately. If it is finite, any strict inequality c>sum_i ρ_i^(s+1) would be contradicted by choosing ε smaller than their positive difference. Thus c≤sum_i ρ_i^(s+1) in all cases. Discharge L2 and quantify V: every δ-cover of F has (s+1)-cost at least c.

produces.statement: Every countable δ-cover of F has total (s+1)-cost at least c=H^s_δ(E).

argument.text: Taking the infimum of the costs in F004 gives H^s_δ(E)≤H^(s+1)_δ(F). Discharge L1 and universally quantify the real s,δ, retaining their positive-range conditions. This proves the exported inequality at every positive scale.

argument.text: Assume L1: D>0. Fix s and assume L2: 0<s<D. E001 gives H^s(E)=∞. N003 gives H^s_δ(E)≤H^(s+1)_δ(F) for every δ>0. Taking suprema over positive δ yields ∞=H^s(E)≤H^(s+1)(F), so the latter is infinite. Equivalently, for every finite bound there is a scale with the left content above that bound, and all smaller scales have at least as large a content, because shrinking the admissible cover class can only increase an infimum. This explicitly justifies the small-scale limiting assertion of the supplied proof. E001 with exponent s+1 gives dim_H F≥s+1. Discharge L2 and quantify s in its range.

argument.text: N001 gives 0<D≤n in the present branch, so D is a finite real number. The supremum of s+1 over 0<s<D is D+1: choose s arbitrarily close to D from below, for example s=D-D/k for integers k>1. F001 therefore gives dim_H F≥D+1. Discharge L1 to obtain precisely the asserted conditional lower bound.

argument.text: For every a>1, dividing I into N equal closed pieces gives diameters 1/N and total a-cost N^(1-a)→0 as positive integers N→∞. These become arbitrarily fine covers with arbitrarily small cost, so H^a(I)=0. E001 implies dim_H I≤a for every a>1, hence dim_H I≤1.

Fix s,δ and assume L1: 0<s<1 and δ>0. Fix W and assume L2: W is a countable δ-cover of I, padded by empty sets if necessary. Put ρ_i=diam(W_i)≤δ. Fix ε and assume L3: ε>0. For each nonempty W_i, its real infimum and supremum exist, and sup W_i-inf W_i≤ρ_i. Enlarge to the open interval (inf W_i-ε·2^(-i-2),sup W_i+ε·2^(-i-2)), of length at most ρ_i+ε·2^(-i-1). Empty members need no enlargement. This constructs the intervals whose existence is F002.

produces.statement: There is a sequence J of open intervals or empty sets with W_i⊆J_i and length(J_i)≤ρ_i+ε·2^(-i-1) for every i; J_i is empty when W_i is empty.

argument.text: Choose J as in F002. Since I⊆union_i J_i, measure monotonicity, M005, M004 and M006 give 1=λ(I)≤λ(union_i J_i)≤sum_i λ(J_i)≤sum_i ρ_i+ε·sum_i 2^(-i-1)=sum_i ρ_i+ε. Subadditivity applies to the countable family without any assumption on the original W_i; only the enclosing intervals are measured. Discharge L3 and use arbitrariness of ε>0. If sum_i ρ_i is infinite the conclusion is immediate; otherwise a positive difference argument yields sum_i ρ_i≥1. For ρ_i>0, since 0<ρ_i≤δ and s-1<0, ρ_i^s=ρ_i·ρ_i^(s-1)≥δ^(s-1)ρ_i. The same inequality is true when ρ_i=0 because both sides are zero. Taking partial sums and then their suprema gives sum_i ρ_i^s≥δ^(s-1)sum_i ρ_i≥δ^(s-1). Discharge L2 and universally quantify W.

argument.text: Taking the infimum in F003 gives H^s_δ(I)≥δ^(s-1). As δ decreases to zero this tends to infinity since 0<s<1. Thus H^s(I)=∞. E001 gives dim_H I≥s for every 0<s<1. Quantifying δ and then s and letting s increase to one yields dim_H I≥1, and F001 gives equality. Discharge L1, obtaining F004 with the whole quantified measure assertion included for later use.

produces.statement: dim_H I=1 and for every real v with 0<v<1, H^v(I)=∞.

argument.text: Choose x0∈E from H001. The map t↦(x0,t) from I into F preserves distances, because sqrt(dist(x0,x0)^2+|t-u|^2)=|t-u|. Here is the cover-based monotonicity argument for this particular isometric embedding, so no separate dimension theorem is tacitly invoked: given any positive scale δ and any countable δ-cover V_i of F, the sets {t∈I:(x0,t)∈V_i} cover I and have diameter at most diam(V_i). Thus for every exponent s>0, H^s_δ(I)≤H^s_δ(F), and taking suprema over δ>0 gives H^s(I)≤H^s(F). By F004, H^s(F)=∞ for all 0<s<1. E001 gives dim_H F≥s for every such s, hence dim_H F≥1. Combined with F004 this proves the two exported dimension assertions. If D=0, this lower bound reads dim_H F≥D+1. The construction of the vertical copy works unchanged for the unique point of Eucl(0); no positive ambient dimension was used.

argument.text: By N001, D is a finite nonnegative real number. If D>0, N004 gives dim_H F≥D+1. If D=0, N005 gives dim_H F≥1=D+1; these alternatives exhaust D≥0. N002 gives dim_H F≤D+1 in every ambient dimension, including n=0. The two inequalities yield dim_H F=D+1. Substituting F=E×[0,1] and D=dim_H E is exactly the claimed equality, with the coordinate-adjoining Euclidean identification fixed in D001 and no norm replacement.
